title: 12 years as a paper prototype, then I used AI to finally turn it into a playable game — here's the workflow
author: Mox___25
selftext:
Around 2014 I started designing a strategy game on paper: hand-cut cards, a hand-drawn hex map, wars around 1600 with pikes, muskets and cannon. I'm not a programmer or an artist, so for 12 years it never left the table. This year AI tools let me finally build it: \*\*Blood and Powder\*\*, a card + hex board strategy game with 6 empires.



How I split the work:



\- \*\*Design, rules and balance: me.\*\* Every card, faction and rule comes from the paper version. AI-vs-AI simulations help me test the balance (thousands of matches to find broken cards).

\- \*\*Code: an AI coding assistant\*\*, working from my rules and playtest notes. I describe what should happen and test it; it writes and fixes the code.

\- \*\*Card art:\*\* a mix of a local Stable Diffusion setup (ComfyUI + SDXL), Gemini and Meta AI, generating several versions per card and picking the best one.

\- \*\*Soldier sprites:\*\* a sheet with every troop type in Gemini, then a video of the figures turning 360° and doing 6 actions, cut into frames. BiRefNet removes the background and Real-ESRGAN sharpens them.

\- \*\*Translations:\*\* English and Chinese drafted with AI, then a review pass for the game's own terms.



What I learned: the AI is great at volume (1,000+ cards, hundreds of sprites), but the game only got fun once I treated the output like a draft. Consistency (same uniform, same scale, no modern helmets on 1600 soldiers) took more time than generating.



It's free in the browser, no sign-up: [https://sangreypolvora.com/?idioma=en](https://sangreypolvora.com/?idioma=en)



Happy to go deeper into any part of the workflow
